definition.text: An enzyme that a cell secretes and that works outside it, most often to break down large molecules.

facts.text: Breaking macromolecules into small pieces lets their constituents pass through the cell membrane and be used inside the cell.
Bacteria and fungi digest nutrients in their surroundings this way; once inside, the nutrients are processed with help from endoenzymes.
In soil they target carbohydrates (cellulases), lignin (oxidases), organic phosphates (phosphatases), amino sugar polymers (chitinases) and proteins (proteases).
Grouped as hydrolases, lyases, oxidoreductases and transferases, they control soil enzyme activity by degrading biopolymers.
Fungi used in bioremediation secrete oxidative exoenzymes, such as laccases, from their growing hyphal tips.
Cell-free microbial exoenzymes can also clean up pollution, but they are often less robust and hard to introduce into soil.
The word 'exoenzyme' entered English in 1908; pepsin and trypsin were probably the first known.

definition.text: The secretion by fungi of enzymes that break down complex organic matter outside the cell; most such enzymes in leaf litter and soil come from fungi.

facts.text: Making and secreting enzymes is energy-intensive, so evolution favours limiting production.
Some exoenzymes are made constitutively at low levels and boosted when their substrate is plentiful, while glucose represses cellulase production.
Soil pH, temperature, moisture and litter type and quality alter enzyme expression and activity, and fertilizer and tillage shift it through the profile.
In decaying litter, cellulose and other labile substrates go first; lignin is depolymerised later as oxidative enzyme activity rises.
Cellulose is cut by hydrolytic endoglucanases, cellobiohydrolase and β-glucosidase; lignin by phenol oxidases, peroxidases and laccases.
Lignin peroxidase and manganese peroxidase are the hallmark of basidiomycetes and are used to gauge their activity.
Enzyme activity serves as an indicator of soil quality.

title: Soil enzyme assays
article: Fungal extracellular enzyme activity#Measuring fungal extracellular enzyme activity in soil, plant litter, and other environmental samples

definition.text: Laboratory methods that estimate enzyme activity in soil or litter by mixing samples with buffers and a substrate.

facts.text: Hydrolytic enzymes are measured colorimetrically with p-nitrophenol-linked substrates or fluorometrically with 4-methylumbelliferone-linked ones.
Phenol oxidase is measured by oxidation of L-DOPA, pyrogallol or ABTS; peroxidase is the difference when the same assay is rerun with hydrogen peroxide added.
Results depend on sample transport and storage, assay pH, substrate concentration, temperature and sample preparation.
Assays mostly reveal exo-acting enzymes that cut from chain ends; molecular methods now count enzyme-coding genes to link enzymes with their producers.

definition.text: An enzyme that frees attached phosphate groups from other molecules, working best at acidic pH.

facts.text: It hydrolyses a phosphate monoester with water to give an alcohol and phosphate, at an optimum pH below 7.
Soil microorganisms use phosphatase enzymes to reach organically bound phosphate.
Assays of phosphatase activity can reveal the biological demand for phosphate in a soil.
Some roots, especially cluster roots, exude carboxylates with acid phosphatase activity that mobilise phosphorus in nutrient-poor soils.

definition.text: An enzyme that hydrolyses terminal β-D-glucosyl residues, releasing glucose.

facts.text: Together with cellulases (endoglucanases) and cellobiosidases it is needed to consume cellulose, a polymer of β-1,4-linked glucose.
It finishes cellulose breakdown by splitting cellobiose into glucose; removing cellobiose also relieves its inhibition of other cellulose enzymes.
Both white- and brown-rot fungi secrete it, and it can also cleave xylose, mannose and galactose.
Soil and litter assays track cellulose degradation through cellobiohydrolase and β-glucosidase activity on pNP or MUF substrates.

definition.text: A heme-containing peroxidase enzyme, one of the ligninases, that uses hydrogen peroxide to cleave lignin-like compounds.

facts.text: Lignin resists biodegradation so strongly that only higher fungi and some bacteria can break it down, by oxidation.
Fungi such as Phanerochaete chrysosporium produce it to degrade lignin.
It works with veratryl alcohol, a secondary metabolite of white-rot fungi that acts as its cofactor.
Despite twenty years of study, its mechanism is not yet fully elucidated.

definition.text: A heme peroxidase enzyme that uses hydrogen peroxide to oxidise manganese(II) to manganese(III).

facts.text: White-rot fungi secrete it to degrade lignin; discovered in Phanerochaete chrysosporium in 1985, it seems unique to Basidiomycota.
Unstable Mn(III) is released as a chelate with a carboxylic acid, most commonly oxalate.
The Mn(III) oxidises phenolic compounds in lignin directly and can cleave alkyl–aryl bonds.
Rising extracellular Mn(II) and hydrogen peroxide up-regulate it, and lignin also induces it.

definition.text: A sugar molecule in which a hydroxyl group has been replaced by an amine group.

facts.text: More than 60 are known; one of the most abundant, N-acetyl-D-glucosamine, is the main component of chitin.
Soil microbes break down amino sugar polymers with chitinases.
Decomposing plant material yields simpler forms, including sugars and amino sugars, that become microbial biomass or humic assemblages.

definition.text: A piece of DNA that is the source or product of amplification or replication.

facts.text: Amplicons are made artificially by the polymerase or ligase chain reaction, so the term is used interchangeably with 'PCR product'.
Bacteria and archaea can be classified by comparing amplicons of the highly conserved 16S rRNA gene with known sequences.
Fungi are classified the same way from the 18S rRNA gene and the ITS1 region.
In amplicon sequencing, counts of identical taxa give their relative abundance in the sample.

definition.text: DNA or RNA barcoding done so that many taxa in one sample are identified at once.

facts.text: Unlike barcoding, it aims at the species composition of a sample, passing through DNA extraction, PCR amplification, sequencing and data analysis.
Soil can be a bulk sample of collected organisms or a source of environmental DNA taken without separating the organisms.
Soil contains inhibitors, so special techniques are needed to isolate its DNA.
There is not yet consensus on the best experimental design and bioinformatics criteria.

definition.text: A microbial ecology technique that traces nutrient uptake by microorganisms by feeding them substrate enriched in a heavy stable isotope.

facts.text: Biomarkers carrying the heavy isotope are separated from unlabelled ones by isopycnic centrifugation.
With 13CO2, labelled DNA is spun out and sequenced to show which organisms use freshly made photosynthate; 18O-water shows which are actively growing.
13C is used most often; 15N gives a weaker DNA density shift because DNA holds fewer nitrogen atoms.
Because the density shift is predictable, quantitative SIP (qSIP) can estimate how much isotope was incorporated.

definition.text: The study of how the balance of energy and elements affects living systems, and how organisms affect that balance.

facts.text: Like chemical stoichiometry it rests on mass balance, an idea traced to Liebig, Lotka and Redfield.
A mismatch between what organisms need and what their food holds is an elemental imbalance: termites have tissue C:N of about 5 but eat wood of 300–1000.
Plants have weak stoichiometric homeostasis and vary widely in composition, while animals keep close to a fixed composition.
It has been applied to nutrient recycling, resource competition, animal growth and nutrient limitation in whole ecosystems.
A 2007 study found global average C:N:P ratios of 186:13:1 in soil and 60:7:1 in soil microbial biomass.
The growth rate hypothesis holds that phosphorus demand rises during active growth, to build P-rich nucleic acids.

definition.text: The simplest model of enzyme kinetics, for reactions that turn one substrate into one product.

facts.text: Its equation gives the rate as v = Va/(Km + a), where V (Vmax) is the limiting rate at saturating substrate concentration.
The Michaelis constant Km is the substrate concentration at which the rate is half of V.
Michaelis and Menten published the theory in 1913, building on Victor Henri's 1902 equation.
Copiotrophic microbes have a higher Michaelis–Menten constant than oligotrophs.

definition.text: A process in which microorganisms turn dissolved organic carbon into refractory forms that resist further microbial degradation.

facts.text: In the ocean it can lock carbon away for centuries to millennia, unlike the biological pump, which relies on sinking particles.
A conceptual model of the same name describes how soil microorganisms transform and stabilise soil organic matter.
In it, microbial carbon is either respired to the atmosphere or enters the stable pool as microbial necromass.
Under ocean warming, extra carbon is converted to CO2 rather than used to build new microbial biomass.

definition.text: A unitless measure of temperature sensitivity: the factor by which a reaction rate changes for a 10 °C rise.

facts.text: It assumes rates depend exponentially on temperature, with Q10 = (R2/R1)^(10 °C/(T2−T1)), and applies to processes such as respiration and photosynthesis.
For most biological systems Q10 is about 2 to 3: rates double or triple with every 10 °C.
Environmental scientists often take 0 °C or 10 °C as the reference temperature.
The idea is thought to come from van 't Hoff's work in the late 19th century.

definition.text: All the antibiotic resistance genes in communities of pathogenic and non-pathogenic bacteria.

facts.text: Soil metagenomes from urban, agricultural and forest sites showed spore-forming soil bacteria resistant to most major antibiotics.
In soil, resistance genes sit on mobile genetic elements, making soil and water communities reservoirs from which resistance can pass to pathogens.
Sequencing has shown resistance genes exchanged between soil bacteria and clinical pathogens, some matching exactly across five antibiotic classes.
Sequences from ancient permafrost show antibiotic resistance existed millennia before human-made antibiotics.

definition.text: The living microbes of soil and their metabolites, a few percent of soil organic matter with a short residence time.

facts.text: Temperate grassland soils have held 1–2 t/ha of bacterial and 2–5 t/ha of fungal biomass.
Microbial biomass can be estimated by weighing soil before and after fumigation.
Microbes compete with plants for inorganic nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, tying them up in their biomass: immobilization.
Microbial biomass is a reservoir of stored soil carbon, one way soil microbes sequester carbon.
Soil microbial biomass averages a C:N:P ratio of 60:7:1 worldwide.
Tillage can immediately cut microbial biomass carbon and nitrogen, while cover crops raised microbial biomass carbon by roughly 20% in a meta-analysis.
Microbial biomass and activity are standard measures of soil health.

definition.text: A measure of how much of the carbon a microbe takes up goes into biomass rather than into maintenance energy.

facts.text: Copiotrophs tend to have lower carbon use efficiency than oligotrophs, so they make less protein per gram of oxygen consumed.
In soil, the balance between catabolism that releases carbon as CO2 and anabolism that builds stable carbon compounds controls net carbon retention.

definition.text: A method of measuring the quantity of a substance by adding a known amount of an isotopically enriched form of it to the sample.

facts.text: The enriched standard dilutes the sample's isotopic composition; the method works from signal ratios, not intensities, and is an internal standardisation method, giving it very high metrological standing.
It is almost always paired with mass spectrometry, is used by national metrology institutes to certify reference materials, and helps when analyte recovery is low.
In gas chromatography it can cut uncertainty from 5% to 1%; isotope dilution mass spectrometry measures ratios to better than 0.25%.
Double (reverse) dilution first calibrates the enriched spike against a natural-composition standard, because spikes come in small amounts of questionable purity.
The principle is analogous to mark-and-recapture population estimates in ecology.

definition.text: Mass spectrometry that measures the relative abundance of isotopes in a sample, used for stable-isotope and radiogenic-isotope studies.

facts.text: Stable-isotope analysis measures variations from mass-dependent fractionation, while radiogenic analysis measures decay products and underpins most long-lived radiometric dating.

Magnetic sector instruments are preferred over quadrupoles because they allow multiple-collector analysis and give good peak shapes; ions are accelerated, bent by mass-to-charge ratio and counted in Faraday cups.
Light elements such as H, C and O are measured as pure gases from combustion, GC or chemical trapping against standards; carbon uses VPDB and oxygen uses V-SMOW.
Thermal ionization MS suits low-ionization elements like Sr and Pb, while MC-ICP-MS reaches elements such as Hf-W and Lu-Hf that TIMS cannot; quadrupole ICP-MS precision is only about 1%.

definition.text: An isotope-ratio technique for isotopes at extremely low levels, which accelerates negative ions through a mega-volt potential.

facts.text: Charge exchange removes interfering species and energy-loss detectors separate ions of the same mass-to-charge ratio, allowing isotope ratios above 10^12.
It extended 14C dating to about 60,000 years BP and is about 10^6 times more sensitive than conventional IRMS.
